name: Manmade Anomaly Undersea Dataset (MAUD)
description: Cost-effective undersea monitoring is critical to both the defense community and environmental stakeholders, where detecting anthropogenic objects in coastal and reef environments serves as the first line of defense for risk management and biosecurity. However, while vision is an economical sensing modality, it is severely degraded in the undersea environment through wavelength-dependent absorption, backscatter, and caustics. Existing underwater datasets compound this problem by framing detection categorically, over a fixed catalog of found objects, evaluated on pooled, non-continuous data. Visual anomaly detection better matches this problem’s single-class nature, but has been developed almost entirely on static, fixedcamera settings. There is a need for a dataset that pairs deliberately controlled anomalies with continuously-traversing video imagery simulating real autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) and remotely operated vehicle (ROV) deployments. This thesis addresses this need with two contributions. The first is the Manmade Anomaly Undersea Dataset (MAUD): 113 video clips across five sites in St. John, U.S. Virgin Islands, spanning varied habitats and fourteen anomaly subtypes deliberately placed along a planned diver path.
